source_read: PMC HTML, PMC5710622 (the published JAMA Pediatrics article, 2017;171(10):948-956); page title confirmed in my own tab. Whole text read with get_page_text (53,791 characters, complete): Key Points, abstract, all sections, Tables 1 and 2 (as text), figure legends and reference list; the collapsed article notes (author contributions, conflict of interest disclosures) read from the page. This PMC rendering shows no in-text citation numbers. Figure 2 (special populations) and Figure 1 (map) looked at on screen. Supplement (eTables 1-6, eMethods, eFigures 1-2; PDF) not read. For the card check only: PROSPERO CRD42016033837 and the authors' JAMA Pediatrics reply (doi 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2018.0058, opening paragraph, read on the second attempt after a check page) were read at the stated place.

claims.note: This source supports only the dating: the search covered studies from 1 November 1973, 'when FAS was first described'. No citation can be seen at that phrase, because this PMC rendering prints no in-text citation numbers anywhere. The reference list does include Jones KL and Smith DW, 'Recognition of the fetal alcohol syndrome in early infancy', Lancet 1973;302(7836):999-1001 (reference 21). So 'one of them citing a later 1973 paper' is right for the companion review (Popova et al. 2017, reference 13), and this review may cite the same paper too, though where cannot be seen. The PROSPERO record of this review gives January 1973 instead (registry, not the paper).

anchors.locator: Abstract > Data Sources; Methods > Comprehensive Systematic Search Strategy, 1st paragraph; References, 21
anchors.extracted: Databases searched for studies published from 1 November 1973 (when FAS was first described) to 30 June 2015, without geographic or language restriction. Reference 21: Jones KL, Smith DW, Recognition of the fetal alcohol syndrome in early infancy, Lancet 1973;302(7836):999-1001 (no in-text citation markers rendered on PMC).

claims.overstatement: None in direction. The claim presents the world and regional figures as model estimates and the 1-in-13 ratio as an average, not a per-pregnancy risk, which is more careful than the Key Points ('approximately 8 of 1000 in the general population had FASD'). No amounts read as advice.
claims.note: Not supported: 'eight select studies' of special populations. Figure 2 and its legend show nine: Swedish adoptees from Eastern Europe 521.1; US foster and adopted youth at a mental health centre 285.2; Canadian correctional population 233.5; Canadian aboriginal population 189.7; South African rural low-income population 182.4; Brazilian orphanage 170.2; US psychiatric care 142.4; Australian aboriginal population 120.4; Israeli children before adoption or in foster care 40.0 (references 66-74). The range 40.0 to 521.1 per 1,000 and the multiples 5.2 to 67.7 are right (40.0 / 7.7 = 5.2; 521.1 / 7.7 = 67.7), so change 'eight' to 'nine' in the statement and the magnitude. Everything else from Lange checks: 24 studies, 1,416 children and youth (recomputed from Table 1), ages 0-16.4, 8 countries; 7.7 (4.9-11.7) per 1,000 and the six regional figures (Table 2); the five highest countries with method flags; 76 of 187 above 1%; 1 in 13; about 630,000 a year; pooled for 6 countries (Australia, Croatia, France, Italy, South Africa, USA; 181 others predicted, including single-study Canada and Norway); every Table 1 value quoted, with the Reunion row printed 66.0 although 75/1,320 = 56.8 (as the claim says); the three stated limitations; conflicts 'None reported' and no funding note. Recomputed: 9.8% / 13 = 7.5 per 1,000; 630,000 / 365 = 1,726 a day (the paper's 'more than 1700'); 7.7 per 1,000 x 81,536,534 live births = 627,831. Qualifiers the claim could add. (1) Studies were eligible if they measured FASD 'or a combination of any of the diagnoses within the spectrum' (breakdown only in eTable 2). The lowest figures, from newborn clinic studies and the national Australian study, may therefore count only part of the spectrum. (2) The ratio of 13 came only from countries with a WHO drinking-pattern score of 3 or less; countries scoring 4 or more were left out as giving an 'unrealistically high ratio', but the ratio was then applied to them too. The main text does not say which countries entered it. (3) The authors judged publication bias unlikely in advance and would not have adjusted for it. (4) One included study used passive surveillance in part, despite the exclusion rule. (5) Two newer South African studies (170 to 259 per 1,000) fell outside the search window.

anchors.extracted: 24 unique studies, 1,416 children and youth with FASD, ages 0-16.4; no studies of adults; 8 countries: Australia 2, Canada 1, Croatia 2, France 4, Italy 2, Norway 1, South Africa 6, USA 6 studies. 18 active case ascertainment (75.0%), 5 clinic-based (20.8%), 1 mixed methods (4.2%); 45.8% used the clarified Institute of Medicine criteria.

anchors.locator: Table 2; Results > Prevalence of FASD Among Children and Youth in the General Population, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: FASD per 1,000 children and youth, 2012: African 7.8 (5.4-10.7); Eastern Mediterranean 0.1 (0.1-0.5); European 19.8 (14.1-28.0); Americas 8.8 (6.4-13.2); South-East Asia 1.4 (0.6-5.3); Western Pacific 6.7 (4.5-11.7); global 7.7 (4.9-11.7). Highest: South Africa 111.1 (71.1-158.4; meta-analysis), Croatia 53.3 (30.9-81.2; meta-analysis), Ireland 47.5 (28.0-73.6; prediction), Italy 45.0 (35.1-56.1; meta-analysis), Belarus 36.6 (23.7-53.2; prediction). 76 of 187 countries above 1%. 1 in 13 pregnant women who drank estimated to deliver a child with FASD; about 630,000 born a year.

Study-level FASD per 1,000: Australia 0.1 (national; 92 in 1,533,333, i.e. 0.06) and 1.7 (Northern Territory, mixed methods); Canada 5.3; Croatia 40.8 and 66.8; France 0.4, 5.4 and 5.6 (newborns, clinic-based) and 66.0 (Reunion Island, active ascertainment; 75/1,320 = 56.8); Italy 40.5 and 47.1; Norway 1.1; South Africa 89.0, 89.2, 207.5, 175.0, 88.0 and 63.9 (Western and Northern Cape, active ascertainment, ages 4.8-16.4); USA 25.0, 7.0, 21.9, 33.5, 11.1 and 5.1. Cases sum to 1,416.

anchors.locator: Methods > Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph; Methods > Prevalence Estimation, 1st paragraph; Methods > Global and Regional Estimates, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Random-effects pooling (Freeman-Tukey) for countries with 2 or more studies; publication bias judged unlikely in advance and not adjusted. Countries with 1 or no study: Popova et al.'s drinking-in-pregnancy prevalence divided by a quotient of women who drank per FASD case, derived only from countries with a WHO drinking-pattern score of 3 or less (score 4 or more excluded as an unrealistically high ratio); Monte Carlo intervals (1 million samples). Regional and global means weighted by live births (latest year 2000-2014).

anchors.locator: Results > Comparison of the Global Prevalence of FASD ... With the Prevalence in Special Populations, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 and legend
anchors.extracted: Nine select special-population studies (Figure 2 bars, references 66-74): 521.1, 285.2, 233.5, 189.7, 182.4, 170.2, 142.4, 120.4 and 40.0 per 1,000. As multiples of 7.7: aboriginal 15.6-24.6, children in care 5.2-67.7, correctional 30.3, low socioeconomic status 23.7, psychiatric care 18.5 (all reproduce).

anchors.locator: Methods > Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria; Discussion > Strengths and Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Eligible studies measured FASD or any combination of diagnoses within the spectrum, with a stated guideline or case definition, by active ascertainment or clinic-based methods; passive surveillance excluded (yet one included study used mixed passive and clinic methods). Limitations: self-reported drinking may be underestimated; different diagnostic guidelines; studies not nationally representative, some where FASD was more prevalent; predicted values carry error; timing, dose and frequency not examinable. Diagnostic systems lack reliability (low convergent validity). Two newer South African studies (170-259 per 1,000) not included.

reporting_issues.note: Trivial: rural Croatia (55/824 = 66.75) prints 66.8 where 66.7 is the strict rounding, and the national Australian row (0.06) prints 0.1; otherwise every row reproduces. 66.0 would need about 1,136 children (75 / 0.066).
Likely resolution on the Popova side: 3191 per 10,000 read as 319.1 per 10,000 (31.9 per 1,000) fits Popova's 'more than 14 times' and lies below this paper's 170.2 per 1,000 FASD figure.
Checked on PMC (article notes carry contributions and disclosures, no funding note); the JAMA article page was not checked by me.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low follows from items 2 (PROSPERO CRD42016033837 registered on 31 January 2016, review start 1 May 2015, after the search closed in June 2015; confirmed in the record) and 7 alone. Item 6 'yes' is generous: the Methods name only one author (S.L.), who checked the extracted data, and do not say who extracted them, so 'no' is also defensible. The overall rating is unchanged.

missed: This PMC rendering shows no in-text citation numbers at all, so the source of 'when FAS was first described' (1 November 1973) cannot be seen, although Jones and Smith (1973), Lancet 302:999-1001, is reference 21. Relevant to cl_alc_fas_first_description, together with the PROSPERO record's 'January 1973'.

The authors' reply (key finding 10) places the two Italian studies in 'central Italy' and 'the Lazio region', while Table 1 labels both 'Italy (Lazio)'. Lazio is in central Italy, so this may be loose wording, not a conflict.

A question needing outside data (live births by country, not in the paper). Key finding 5's note puts the small gaps between Table 2 and drinking / 13 down to the six meta-analysed countries. Yet the African figure (7.8) is almost exactly 10.0% / 13 = 7.7, which would require South Africa's meta-analysed 111.1 per 1,000 to carry only about 0.1% of the region's weighted births. As with the companion paper's FAS figures, the regional means may not include the meta-analysed values; eTable 4 would settle it.
